newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-Soothing senators.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-Soothing senators.

text.p: BY Jim Middleton (ABC TV Political Correspondent)
The power of one -- plus one.
Playing the avuncular role to the hilt, Brian Harradine always likes to appear the innocent whenever it's suggested he has the power to make or break government legislation.
He just one of 75 senators, he protests. They're all just as powerful as he is. But that is not the case.

Telstra was the most spectacular, but far from the only, example that some senators are more equal than others. Senator Harradine and his recent comrade in arms, fellow Labor renegade Mal Colston, have got muscle and they keep on using it.

This week it was Senator Harradine's turn, humbling Health Minister Michael Wooldridge over the long delayed appointment of a new head of the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), the nation's premier health research body.

Wooldridge wanted to appoint Professor John Funder from the Baker Medical Research Institute in Melbourne to the post. But back in 1990, Professor Funder wrote a discussion paper for the NHMRC in favour of testing of the so-called morning-after pill RU 486, a drug the anti-abortion Senator Harradine abhors.

Sticking to the script he always employs in such circumstances, the Tasmanian Senator denied he'd "vetoed" Dr Wooldridge's choice. He did admit he'd passed on representations to the government about the NHMRC post but would not reveal what they were.
Whatever -- the man whom the health minister had made no secret was his favourite, the man to whom his department had sent a draft contract, suddenly found himself out of favour.
The overwhelming support of the health research community did Professor Funder no good either.
On Wednesday afternoon, Dr Wooldridge announced the appointment of Professor Richard Larkins from Melbourne University.
Professor Larkins acknowledged his own embarrassment.
"It's been difficult for me because I didn't have it in mind that this would be a particular job that I'd be doing," he said.
Australian Medical Association chief Keith Woollard and eminent researcher David Penington both claimed politics had sullied the credibility of the NHMRC.
Dr Wooldridge admitted he'd been rolled in cabinet: "It's not my decision. It's cabinet's decision..." was his wistful comment.
That's not all. Informed sources suggest the prime minister assured Senator Harradine before Tuesday's cabinet decision that Professor Funder would not be appointed.
What did the Senator and the prime minister have to say when asked about such an assurance by ABC TV news?
There was no direct denial from either man. Howard's office refused to go beyond stating: "The government has nothing to add."

No direct rebuttal from Senator Harradine either: "Do you expect me to say that the Prime Minister would be able to tell me there is going to be a particular appointment before cabinet has made a judgement?"

So a man who would present himself as a simple senator from Tasmania -- a person with no more power than his 74 colleagues -- has knocked off a respected health minister, the leadership of the medical profession and the Australian research community.

Not bad, but for what? Well, the next budget is just around the corner and as last year the government needs the votes of Senators Harradine and Colston to ensure its major initiatives survive the Senate.

Such votes do not come cheap. According to the Opposition, the price tag for Senator Colston's Telstra vote was A$75,000. That's Senate officers' estimate of the money required to meet Senator Colston's pre-vote demand to the government for upgrading of his staff.

Senate President Margaret Reid, a Liberal, initially rejected the Colston ultimatum. He insisted she make the request to the prime minister. She did, but made it clear she had no enthusiasm for the idea. Howard thought otherwise -- approving the demand with alacrity and citing Senator Reid in support to boot.

Not that previous governments behaved much differently. Labor did its best to soothe Senator Harradine. Devout Catholic Michael Tate was frequently assigned to find out what the Senator wanted -- how to ease his concerns, what it would take to secure his vote.
With the budget season upon us, no wonder John Howard is just as sensitive to the independent Senators' needs and concerns.
As ever, some Senators are more equal than others.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
